plan.name: Marathon Training: Intermediate 2
plan.author: Hal Higdon
plan.description: An 18-week marathon plan for experienced runners, starting with a 10-mile long run and building to three 20-mile long runs.

meta.target_audience: Experienced marathoners ready for higher mileage than Intermediate 1

cross_training.label: Cross Training
cross_training.description: A non-running aerobic session used to maintain fitness while reducing running impact.

easy_run.label: Easy Run
easy_run.description: An easy aerobic run done at a comfortable, conversational pace to build endurance while limiting fatigue.

long_run.label: Long Run
long_run.description: The key to the program is the long run on weekends, which builds from 10 miles in the first week to a maximum of 20 miles. Although some experienced runners do train longer, I see no advantage in doing 23, 26 or even 31 mile runs. (I've tried that myself in the past, and it just wore me out.) Save your energy and concentrate on quality runs the rest of the week. Consistency is most important. You can skip an occasional workout, or juggle the schedule depending on other commitments, but do not cheat on the long runs. Notice that although the weekly long runs get progressively longer, every third week is a "stepback" week, where we reduce mileage to allow you to gather strength for the next push upward. Rest is an important component of any training program.

pace_run.label: Pace Run
pace_run.description: A run done at planned race pace to practice rhythm, pacing control, and race-specific effort.

rest.label: Rest
rest.description: A no-training day used to absorb prior workouts and promote recovery.

coaching_guidance.text: The key to the program is the long run on weekends, which builds from 10 miles in the first week to a maximum of 20 miles. Although some experienced runners do train longer, I see no advantage in doing 23, 26 or even 31 mile runs. (I've tried that myself in the past, and it just wore me out.) Save your energy and concentrate on quality runs the rest of the week. Consistency is most important. You can skip an occasional workout, or juggle the schedule depending on other commitments, but do not cheat on the long runs. Notice that although the weekly long runs get progressively longer, every third week is a "stepback" week, where we reduce mileage to allow you to gather strength for the next push upward. Rest is an important component of any training program.
Keep most long runs conversational, generally at least 30–90 seconds per mile slower than goal marathon pace.
Experienced runners may occasionally pick up the pace for the final quarter of a long run if they still feel fresh. Higdon suggests using this approach at most once every three weeks.
Walk briefly as needed, including at aid stations, and practice doing so on training runs.
Use your planned marathon pace for the prescribed pace runs.
Use an easy aerobic activity such as swimming, cycling or walking on Mondays.
Run most Tuesday through Thursday miles comfortably. The midweek distance builds along with the Sunday long run.
Rest on Fridays before Saturday pace work and Sunday long runs.
The schedule emphasizes endurance and practicing marathon pace. It does not include dedicated speedwork.
